title: Solids of Revolution
body:
Take a region in the plane, spin it about a line, and ask for the volume of the solid it sweeps
out. Three formulas get taught and **they are one idea**: slice the solid, find the area of a
slice, integrate the area along the slicing direction. It is the [[Riemann Sum]] again with a
different rectangle.

$$
V = \int_a^b A(x)\,dx
$$

Everything below is just what $A(x)$ turns out to be.

## Disk and washer

Slice **perpendicular** to the axis of rotation. Each slice is a circle, or a circle with a circle
punched out of it.

$$
V_{\text{disk}} = \pi\int_a^b \left[R(x)\right]^2 dx
\qquad
V_{\text{washer}} = \pi\int_a^b \left(\left[R(x)\right]^2 - \left[r(x)\right]^2\right) dx
$$

$R$ is the distance from the axis to the far edge of the region, $r$ to the near edge. **It is
$R^2 - r^2$, never $(R-r)^2$.** That is the mistake, and it is the same one as thinking the area of
an annulus is the area of a circle of width $R-r$.

## Cylindrical shells

Slice **parallel** to the axis instead. Each slice is a thin rectangle that sweeps out a hollow
cylinder; unroll it and it is a sheet of area $2\pi \cdot \text{radius} \cdot \text{height}$.

$$
V_{\text{shell}} = 2\pi\int_a^b (\text{radius})(\text{height})\,dx
$$

For rotation about the $y$-axis with the region under $y = f(x)$ on $[a,b]$, that is
$2\pi\int_a^b x f(x)\,dx$: radius $x$, height $f(x)$.

## Which one

| | Disk / washer | Shell |
|---|---|---|
| slices are | perpendicular to the axis | parallel to the axis |
| integrate in | the variable **along** the axis | the variable **across** the axis |
| you need the curve solved for | the variable perpendicular to the axis | the variable it is already solved for |

**Pick the one that does not make you invert the function.** Rotating $y = x^3+x$ on $[0,2]$ about
the $y$-axis by washers means solving $y = x^3+x$ for $x$, which cannot be done in any pleasant
way; by shells it is $2\pi\int_0^2 x(x^3+x)\,dx$ and takes a line. A washer setup with a hole means
two functions and a subtraction; a shell setup with a hole often means one integral.

The other reliable check: **draw the slice on the picture** and see whether it is a disk or a
rectangle. If the slice is parallel to the axis, no amount of algebra makes the disk formula right.

## Rotating about a line that is not an axis

Rotating about $x = c$ or $y = c$ changes only the radius. Distance to the axis becomes $|x - c|$
rather than $x$, and for a washer both $R$ and $r$ shift. Nothing else about the setup moves, which
is worth knowing because it looks like a new case in the textbook and is not.

## Related

- [[Integral]] and [[Riemann Sum]] in [[CALCULUS 1]] for the slicing construction
- [[Applications of Integration]]: work, pressure, and centroids are the same slice-and-sum pattern
  applied to physics instead of geometry
- [[Arc Length]], and the surface area of a solid of revolution, which is arc length times
  $2\pi(\text{radius})$ for the same reason a shell is height times circumference
- [[Integration Techniques]]: the integrand is usually a polynomial here, but a rotated
  $\sqrt{\cdot}$ region lands you in [[Integration By Trigonometric Substitution]] fast
- [[Double Integral]] and [[Multiple Integration]] in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]: the general answer
  to "volume of a solid", of which these three formulas are the rotationally symmetric special case
